steps.title: POST /download/video-audio
steps.detail: The client sends a list of URLs with matching file names, a provider string and a download_strategie. One request can carry several URLs — they become one job with one context per file.

steps.title: require_user
steps.detail: Runs as a FastAPI dependency before the handler body. See the Authentication flow for what happens inside.

steps.title: Create task_id and Session
steps.detail: The task_id is the handle the client uses for every follow-up call. The Session carries the cookie jar into the engine, which is why a login harvested by the browser layer survives across the request.

steps.title: _resolveProviderSearchFunction
steps.detail: utils.validateProviders() turns the string into a ProviderTypes value, then PROVIDER_GETRESULTS_MAPPING looks up the function. Two separate failure points: the alias does not resolve, or it resolves but has no entry in the mapping.

steps.title: Resolve every URL in parallel
steps.detail:
One ProviderResultRequest per URL, all dispatched at once through asyncio.gather, each one under the search_limiter semaphore and in a worker thread. This is where the engine takes over: the provider loads the page, sniffs with the browser or asks the YouTube player API, and scores the candidates. A browser-based provider will really open Chromium here, so this step dominates the response time.

The engine also measures the candidate: getUrlInformation() asks for the size of the video URL and, if the provider found a separate audio track, of the audio URL too.

steps.title: Build one DownloadContext per file
steps.sub: target + info + output, total size preset
steps.detail:
Each ProviderResult becomes a DownloadContext with context_id = "{task_id}-{filename}". That composite id is what the progress and stream routes take as their second path parameter.

The DownloadTarget now carries audio_url, audio_size and video_size next to the resolved URL, the OutputTarget carries the bare filename and auto_convert, and download_progress.total_bytes is preset from the provider's total size so the first progress poll already has a denominator.

steps.title: Register the ServerJob
steps.detail: Contexts plus session plus the shared download semaphore become a DownloadInformation, wrapped in a ServerJob with a creation timestamp. It lives in memory only — a restart loses every running job, deliberately.

steps.title: download_strategie?
steps.detail: The single branch point of the handler. STREAM keeps nothing on disk and hands back URLs the client pulls from. LOCAL is switched off: the branch raises ValueError before doing anything, which the handler turns into a 400.

steps.title: LOCAL: switched off
steps.detail:
The first line of the LOCAL branch is raise ValueError("Local Download was turned off by administrator because of pending rework"). The code after it — a fire-and-forget _run_local_download task and one progress_url per context — is unreachable but still in place.

The ValueError lands in the first except branch, so the client sees a 400 with the prefix „Invalid type for“.

steps.title: STREAM: per context, HLS or not?
steps.detail: Each context gets a ServerStream stored under job.stream_jobs. What the watch URL looks like depends on the download type.

steps.title: HLS: pre-compute the segment list
steps.detail:
Runs through asyncio.to_thread because it fetches and parses the playlists synchronously. A master playlist is resolved first: MasterHLSDownload.getUrls() picks the video variant and the audio rendition, and both URLs are written back onto context.target. Then IndexHLSDownload builds the video segment list and, if there is an audio URL, a second list for audio.

Both lists are stored on the ServerStream (segments and audio_segments), so every later playlist and segment request is a pure in-memory lookup rather than a second fetch.

steps.title: FILE / UMP: point at the file name
steps.detail: No pre-computation. The stream type is reported as file. When the provider found separate video and audio URLs, the audio URL is passed on as watch_audio_url in the resource.

steps.title: Return DownloadResponse
steps.detail: Every resource carries progress_url, download_url, watch_url, stream_type and watch_audio_url (empty when audio is not separate). The client is expected to use these URLs verbatim rather than assembling them itself.

steps.title: 401 Unauthorized
steps.sub: raised by the dependency, handler never runs
steps.detail: Missing header or a key that does not match. The same message is used for an unknown identifier and a wrong key.

steps.title: Error responses
steps.detail:
The handler catches four families and maps them:

ValueError, TypeError, ArgumentError, ArgumentErrorCompare → 400 with the prefix „Invalid type for“ — this includes the disabled LOCAL strategy. TaskFailedError → 500. DRMProtectedMediaError → 422, which is how an encrypted Soundcloud stream reports itself. Anything else → 500.

Only data is logged in the 400 branch, not the traceback — and UnicodeDecodeError lands there too because it inherits from ValueError.

Validation errors never get this far: DownloadRequest.model_post_init re-raises everything as ValueError, so FastAPI answers a malformed body (unequal urls/filenames, auto_convert without preferred_file) with a 422 before the handler runs.

steps.title: Request arrives with headers
steps.next: which dependency does the route declare?
steps.detail: Three schemes exist and most routes combine two. Which apply is visible on the route in the Endpoints list.

steps.title: require_admin
steps.sub: only on routes that declare it
steps.detail: secrets.compare_digest(key, ADMIN_KEY) against the value from the .env. Constant time, so the key cannot be recovered by timing the response. This guards the server as a whole, not a particular user's data.

steps.title: require_user: headers present?
steps.sub: X-User-Key and Auth must both be non-empty
steps.detail: Two distinct 401 messages here: Missing X-User-Key and Missing Auth header. These are the only auth errors that tell the caller what was wrong.

steps.title: Look the user up by Auth identifier
steps.detail: The Auth header carries the user identifier, the X-User-Key the secret. If no row comes back the response is the generic Invalid user key — deliberately identical to the wrong-key case, so valid identifiers cannot be enumerated through the error message. A WARN line goes to the log queue.

steps.title: Compare the key
steps.detail:
The stored column holds hash_api_key(apikey), the SHA-256 hex digest written at registration.

This is where the two sides disagree. The comparison is compare_digest(request_api_key, row["ApiKey"]): the raw key from the header against the stored digest. Nothing in require_user hashes the incoming key — the unused request_api_key_hash line that used to sit here has been removed rather than wired in. Plaintext against digest never matches, so authentication only succeeds if the client sends the digest itself. Passing hash_api_key(request_api_key) into the call closes it.

steps.title: Return the authenticated user
steps.detail: The plaintext key is attached as _PlainApiKey for the lifetime of this one request, so /get/user can hand it back to the same client. It is never written anywhere.

steps.title: Ownership check inside the handler
steps.detail:
Authentication proves who is calling; this proves the record is theirs. check_user_identifier() compares against a user row, check_owner() against a UserIdentifier column, and owns_record(table, ...) looks the row up first.

owns_record raises ValueError for any table outside OWNED_TABLES — that allowlist is what keeps an unchecked table name out of the SQL string. A new table with a UserIdentifier column is not protected until it is added there.

steps.title: Handler runs
steps.detail: From here the route does its own work. A missing record returns False from the ownership helpers rather than a 404, so the caller cannot tell „does not exist“ from „not yours“.

steps.title: Rejected
steps.detail: 401 means the caller was not identified, 403 that they were identified but the record is not theirs. Both write a WARN line into the log queue with the identifier that was attempted.

steps.title: Client holds a watch_url
steps.detail: /stream/watch/{task_id}/{stream_id}/master.m3u8, handed over in the DownloadResponse. The video and audio segment lists were already computed when the download request was answered.

steps.title: require_user on every HLS route
steps.detail: All HLS routes — master, both index playlists and the segments — declare dependencies=[Security(require_user)]. The player therefore has to send the two headers on every request, including each segment. A plain <video> tag cannot do that; LibVLC and hls.js with a custom loader can.

steps.title: GET .../master.m3u8
steps.detail:
Renders a small master playlist that points back at this server. Without audio segments it contains a single #EXT-X-STREAM-INF entry for /video/index.m3u8. With audio segments it adds an #EXT-X-MEDIA:TYPE=AUDIO rendition for /audio/index.m3u8 and ties the video variant to it through AUDIO="audio".

The bandwidth is a fixed 5000000; the original variant attributes are not carried over.

steps.title: GET .../video/index.m3u8 and .../audio/index.m3u8
steps.detail:
Both go through create_hls_index(). It writes #EXT-X-VERSION:7, a target duration from the longest segment and one #EXTINF plus URL per segment, pointing at /{video|audio}/segment/{n}. The original CDN URLs never reach the player.

A segment with duration 0 is how the engine's parser stores an #EXT-X-MAP init section; it is written back as #EXT-X-MAP:URI=... instead of a media entry. That is what makes fMP4 streams (YouTube's HLS manifests) playable through the proxy.

steps.title: Player pulls each segment
steps.detail:
segment_type selects the list (video or audio; anything else is a 404), segment_id the index in it. The server fetches the segment through file.asyncDownloadYieldSimple() with the stored session and headers and streams it straight through. start_byte and end_byte are passed along, so playlists that address byte ranges inside one file work too.

Nothing is written to disk. The media type is always reported as video/mp2t, whatever the segments actually contain.

steps.title: Not HLS: /stream/download
steps.sub: the one stream route without a key
steps.detail: /stream/download/{task_id}/{stream_id} runs DownloadDispatcher.downloadContextAndYield() and sends the result as an attachment. Its security dependency was removed, so anyone who knows the two ids can fetch the file. The file name in Content-Disposition is {filename}.{preferred_file} when auto_convert is set, otherwise the provider's full_filename.

branches.label: see the CORS note on the overview

steps.title: Cleanup: only by age
steps.detail:
A job and all its streams stay in memory until cleanup_loop() finds it older than 24 hours — see the Server lifecycle flow.

cleanup_download(), which would drop a single stream a while after it was fetched, exists but is not called anywhere. The inner generator in client_download_stream is still named download_and_cleanup, but it only forwards the chunks.

steps.title: 401 or 404
steps.sub: no key, or nothing under these ids
steps.detail: 401 comes from the dependency before the handler runs. 404 means the job or the stream is gone — after a restart, or once the job is older than 24 hours — or the segment index is out of range.

steps.title: uvicorn starts the app
steps.detail:
Everything below runs before the first request is served, and the teardown half runs after the last one.

Before that, at import time, server.py switches Windows to the Proactor event loop so the engine can start ffmpeg subprocesses. The lifespan prints the loop type as its first action.

steps.title: Start the logger task
steps.detail: Producer/consumer: handlers call log_queue.put_nowait() and return immediately, one task does the file I/O. The queue is capped at 5000 entries.

steps.title: Start cleanup_loop
steps.detail: Compares each job's creation_timestamp against time.monotonic() and drops anything older than 24 hours, together with its stream jobs.

steps.title: create_app_tables()
steps.detail: Idempotent, so a fresh database is created on first start and an existing one is left alone. Note that it only creates — a column added to the schema later will not appear in an existing file. There is no migration step.

steps.title: yield — serving requests
steps.detail: Everything in ServerState lives for exactly this window: jobs, stream jobs, both semaphores, the log queue.

steps.title: Shutdown requested
steps.detail: /command is the client-facing way to stop the server; the desktop app uses it when it exits.

steps.title: Cancel both background tasks
steps.detail: Cancellation is immediate. Anything still sitting in log_queue at that moment is not flushed to disk, so the tail of a crash is often missing from the log file.

steps.title: POST /save
steps.sub: one SaveDataRequest with the whole state
steps.detail: The desktop app sends this once, when it exits. Playlists, media, assignments and settings all travel in a single request — nothing is written incrementally during the session.

steps.title: check_owner
steps.detail: Authentication already happened in require_user. This additionally refuses a request that tries to write someone else's data with a valid key.

steps.title: Size limits
steps.detail: Straightforward DoS guards. Exceeding any of them is a 400 before a single row is touched.

steps.title: 1. Upsert media
steps.detail: Every entry in the request is inserted or updated, keyed on the Identifier the client sends. Those identifiers originally came from the create routes, which generate them server-side; /save just writes back what the client holds.

steps.title: 2. Upsert playlists
steps.detail: Name and description are overwritten from the request.

steps.title: 3. Delete orphaned media
steps.detail:
This is what makes /save a full replacement rather than a merge: anything the client did not send is removed. ON DELETE CASCADE takes the matching PlaylistMedias rows with it — and it really fires now that connect_db() sets foreign_keys=ON.

An empty media list therefore deletes all of the user's media. A client that fails to load its data and then exits normally will wipe the account.

steps.title: 4. Delete orphaned playlists
steps.detail: Identical shape to step 3, including the empty-list case.

steps.title: 5. Rebuild the assignments
steps.sub: delete all, re-insert what has both parents
steps.detail: PlaylistMedias is not upserted but rebuilt from scratch. Each row is checked against both parent tables first; a missing parent is skipped with a WARN line instead of failing the request. That is why a stale assignment silently disappears rather than causing an error.

steps.title: 6. Upsert the settings row
steps.sub: download path, dark mode, scan on startup
steps.detail: One row per user, guarded by the UNIQUE on UserIdentifier.

steps.title: commit, or rollback on any error
steps.sub: all six steps in one transaction
steps.detail: Every step runs on one connection inside one transaction, so a failure half way leaves the previous state intact. The except rolls back and answers 400; the outer handler turns anything that escapes into 500.

steps.title: Rejected before any write
steps.detail: Both guards run before the connection is opened, so a rejected save cannot leave partial data behind.
